name: Cybercrime & Internet Measurement
description: Empirical measurement of cybercrime, underground economies, abuse, fraud, and large-scale internet ecosystems.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list (all USENIX Security 2018) show cybercrime and internet measurement spreading across several distinct fronts at once. On the financial side, "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) probed whether a privacy-focused cryptocurrency actually delivered its promised anonymity, while "Plug and Prey? Measuring the Commoditization of Cybercrime via Online Anonymous Markets" (USENIX 2018) measured how attack capabilities were becoming off-the-shelf commodities. In parallel, the email/abuse front opened with "End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks" (USENIX 2018), and the measurement infrastructure front advanced with "Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship" (USENIX 2018), which extended global censorship detection beyond DNS and IP blocking. From the start the area was empirical and data-driven rather than theoretical.

By 2019 the field sharpened around two themes: software supply-chain risk and email-borne fraud. "Small World with High Risks: A Study of Security Threats in the npm Ecosystem" (USENIX 2019) became a heavily cited template for treating a package registry as an attack surface, while a cluster of enterprise-fraud papers — "Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale" and "High Precision Detection of Business Email Compromise" (both USENIX 2019) — shifted phishing research from generic spam toward targeted, high-value impersonation. Threat-intelligence itself came under measurement scrutiny in "Reading the Tea leaves: A Comparative Analysis of Threat Intelligence" (USENIX 2019), a skeptical-empiricism turn that continued into "A different cup of TI? The added value of commercial threat intelligence" (USENIX 2020).

Around 2019-2021 the center of gravity moved strongly toward two engines: the phishing lifecycle and blockchain/smart-contract abuse. "Sunrise to Sunset" and "PhishTime" (both USENIX 2020) measured the end-to-end effectiveness of the anti-phishing ecosystem and its blacklists, turning phishing into a longitudinal, defense-evaluation problem. Meanwhile Ethereum became its own underground economy to be measured: "The Art of The Scam: Demystifying Honeypots in Ethereum Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2019), "Frontrunner Jones and the Raiders of the Dark Forest" (USENIX 2021), and "Smart Contract Vulnerabilities: Vulnerable Does Not Imply Exploited" (USENIX 2021) — the last making the crucial point that measured exploitation matters more than theoretical vulnerability counts. The area also broadened beyond money to human harm with "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" (USENIX 2020).

Most recently the work matures into ecosystem-scale economic studies and a new adversary. "A Large Scale Study of the Ethereum Arbitrage Ecosystem" (USENIX 2023) treats decentralized finance as a full economy to be quantified, and "Malla: Demystifying Real-world Large Language Model Integrated Malicious Services" (USENIX 2024) marks the arrival of LLM-powered cybercrime as a measurable underground market — closing the loop back to the 2018 commoditization theme, now with AI as the commodity.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this area treated cybercrime and abuse as ecosystems to be mapped rather than single bugs to be patched. At NDSS 2018 the community was busy inventorying who watches whom online: "Apps, Trackers, Privacy, and Regulators: A Global Study of the Mobile Tracking Ecosystem" (NDSS 2018) charted the third-party tracking layer baked into mobile apps, while "Bug Fixes, Improvements, ... and Privacy Leaks" (NDSS 2018) followed PII leakage across Android app versions over time. Alongside these privacy censuses sat early studies of abuse plumbing — content-tampering by "A Large-scale Analysis of Content Modification by Open HTTP Proxies" (NDSS 2018), phone-scam defenses in "Towards Measuring the Effectiveness of Telephony Blacklists" (NDSS 2018), and blackhat SEO in "Game of Missuggestions" (NDSS 2018). The common thread was large-scale, empirical observation of systems already misbehaving in the wild.

By 2019-2020 the field turned toward criminal infrastructure and how to disrupt it. IoT botnets became a marquee target with "Measurement and Analysis of Hajime, a Peer-to-peer IoT Botnet" (NDSS 2019) and the remediation study "Cleaning Up the Internet of Evil Things" (NDSS 2019), while takedown mechanics were dissected in "Cracking the Wall of Confinement" (NDSS 2019) and "A Practical Approach for Taking Down Avalanche Botnets" (NDSS 2020). Two shifts stand out. First, researchers began measuring developer- and platform-side exposure directly, as in "How Bad Can It Git? Characterizing Secret Leakage in Public GitHub Repositories" (NDSS 2019). Second, methods grew more active and economic: "Cybercriminal Minds" (NDSS 2019) traced cryptocurrency abuse on the Dark Web, and "Into the Deep Web" (NDSS 2020) went a step further by autonomously chatting with e-commerce fraudsters instead of merely observing their servers.

The 2021-2023 period broadened the definition of "the ecosystem" to include new platforms, regulation, and the arms races around detection. Voice assistants ("Hey Alexa, is this Skill Safe?", NDSS 2021), the post-GDPR domain landscape ("From WHOIS to WHOWAS", NDSS 2021), adblock circumvention ("CV-Inspector", NDSS 2021), and the residential-proxy economy ("Your Phone is My Proxy", NDSS 2021) all became measurement targets. Cryptocurrency crime matured into its own subfield with "Double and Nothing: Understanding and Detecting Cryptocurrency Giveaway Scams" (NDSS 2023), while browser-fingerprinting reached billion-scale characterization in "Him of Many Faces" (NDSS 2023) and internet-scale scanning extended to cyber-physical systems in "ChargePrint" (NDSS 2023).

The most recent NDSS 2026 work shows the area settling into planetary-scale measurement of both abuse infrastructure and the anti-abuse machinery itself. Residential proxies remain a live battleground, now approached with adversarially robust detection in "Beyond RTT: An Adversarially Robust Two-Tiered Approach For Residential Proxy Detection" (NDSS 2026) and traffic-spoofing hygiene in "Aliens Among Us" (NDSS 2026). Social-platform manipulation is measured directly in "TBTrackerX" and "Revealing The Secret Power: How Algorithms Can Influence Content Visibility on Twitter/X" (both NDSS 2026), and researchers increasingly study the defenders — the abuse-reporting and threat-intelligence pipelines — in "Tickets to Hide" and "Actively Understanding the Dynamics and Risks of the Threat Intelligence Ecosystem" (NDSS 2026). Perhaps most emblematic of where the field stands is "Hey there! You are using WhatsApp: Enumerating Three Billion Accounts for Security and Privacy" (NDSS 2026), which turns a single messaging platform into a three-billion-account privacy census — the same mapping instinct that opened the area in 2018, now operating at truly internet scale.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work on this list treats cybercrime as an economy to be followed end to end. "Tracking Ransomware End-to-end" (S&P 2018) traced the full payment path of ransomware from infected hosts through Bitcoin cash-out, putting hard numbers on a criminal business model, while "Surveylance: Automatically Detecting Online Survey Scams" (S&P 2018) built automated infrastructure to find and characterize fraud at scale. Alongside these abuse-economy studies sat a parallel strand of ecosystem hygiene measurement — "Tracking Certificate Misissuance in the Wild" (S&P 2018) and "Enumerating Active IPv6 Hosts for Large-Scale Security Scans via DNSSEC-Signed Reverse Zones" (S&P 2018) — showing that the same empirical, large-scale toolkit could be pointed either at criminals or at the internet's own plumbing.

The field then broadened from tracking money to mapping the hidden infrastructure and human harms around abuse. "Resident Evil: Understanding Residential IP Proxy as a Dark Service" (S&P 2019) exposed a whole gray market of residential proxies that launder malicious traffic, and "PhishFarm" (S&P 2019) turned measurement on the defenders by systematically testing how well browser blacklists resist evasion. By 2020 and 2021 the definition of "cybercrime" itself widened to include interpersonal and societal harm: "The Many Kinds of Creepware Used for Interpersonal Attacks" (S&P 2020) and "SoK: Hate, Harassment, and the Changing Landscape of Online Abuse" (S&P 2021) reframed abuse as something aimed at people, not just machines, while "A First Look at Zoombombing" (S&P 2021) and "TrollMagnifier: Detecting State-Sponsored Troll Accounts on Reddit" (S&P 2022) measured coordinated harassment and influence operations. A distinct compliance-and-governance line also emerged here, with "Do Cookie Banners Respect my Choice?" (S&P 2020) treating regulation itself as a measurable object.

A major breakthrough of the early 2020s was extending measurement into cryptocurrency ecosystems as active adversarial markets rather than passive ledgers. "Quantifying Blockchain Extractable Value: How dark is the forest?" (S&P 2022) — by far the most-cited paper here — quantified how bots extract value by reordering transactions, and "Non-Atomic Arbitrage in Decentralized Finance" (S&P 2024) carried that agenda forward into the interplay between on-chain and off-chain markets. In parallel, abuse detection kept scaling up and out, from "Beyond Phish: Toward Detecting Fraudulent e-Commerce Websites at Scale" (S&P 2023) to supply-chain threats in "Investigating Package Related Security Threats in Software Registries" (S&P 2023).

The most recent work shows the area splitting into two mature directions at once. On the abuse side, detection is getting more adversarial and more graph-aware: "Promoguardian: Detecting Promotion Abuse Fraud with Multi-Relation Fused Graph Neural Networks" (S&P 2026) and "Breaking Free from Ivory Tower: Evaluating and Enhancing Real-world Chinese Underground Adversarial Jargon Detection" (S&P 2026) tackle fraudsters who actively evade classifiers, while "APT to Disagree: A Comparative Analysis of Attribution in Commercial TI" (S&P 2026) turns a critical measurement lens on the threat-intelligence industry itself. On the governance and infrastructure side, the compliance strand from cookie banners has grown into "Setting the Course, but Forgetting to Steer" (S&P 2026) on GDPR access rights and "Consumer Beware! Exploring Data Brokers' CCPA Compliance" (S&P 2026), and internet-ecosystem measurement continues with "The Threat Landscape of IP Leasing in the RPKI Era" (S&P 2026) and "LEAKYLINKS: Measuring the Security and Privacy Risks of URL Scanning Services" (S&P 2026). Taken together, the arc runs from following ransom payments in 2018 to auditing entire abuse markets, regulatory regimes, and security-tooling supply chains in 2026.

ccs.narrative:
Cybercrime and internet measurement at CCS brings empirical rigor to underground economies, abuse ecosystems, and large-scale internet infrastructure. The 2018 cohort documented two emerging abuse categories: MineSweeper (CCS 2018) and How You Get Shot in the Back (CCS 2018) together characterized browser-based cryptojacking as a novel revenue stream for attackers exploiting users' CPU cycles. Detecting Fake Accounts in Online Social Networks at the Time of Registrations (CCS 2019) moved Sybil detection to the enrollment stage before fake accounts cause harm.

Censorship measurement gained infrastructure in 2020: Censored Planet: An Internet-wide, Longitudinal Censorship Observatory (CCS 2020) built a continuous automated platform for tracking global censorship reachability without in-country vantage points. Network hygiene was examined empirically in Network Hygiene, Incentives, and Regulation: Deployment of Source Address Validation in the Internet (CCS 2019).

The cryptocurrency ecosystem attracted intense measurement attention from 2022: Understanding Security Issues in the NFT Ecosystem (CCS 2022) became one of the most-cited papers in the period by characterizing NFT fraud, and Empirical Analysis of EIP-1559: Transaction Fees, Waiting Times, and Consensus Security (CCS 2022) examined how Ethereum's fee-market reform affected real-world behavior and security. TxPhishScope (CCS 2023) brought phishing measurement to on-chain transaction analysis.

milestones.title: MineSweeper: An In-depth Look into Drive-by Cryptocurrency Mining and Its Defense
milestones.note: First in-depth study of browser-based drive-by cryptomining, characterizing the ecosystem and building a behavioral detector.

milestones.title: How You Get Shot in the Back: A Systematical Study about Cryptojacking in the Real World
milestones.note: Systematically measured real-world cryptojacking prevalence and infrastructure across the web.

milestones.title: Network Hygiene, Incentives, and Regulation: Deployment of Source Address Validation in the Internet
milestones.note: Measured global SAV deployment and analyzed the economic and regulatory incentives for spoofing prevention.

milestones.title: Detecting Fake Accounts in Online Social Networks at the Time of Registrations
milestones.note: Detected Sybil accounts at registration time using behavioral signals before accounts could cause harm.

milestones.note: Built an automated internet-wide observatory providing continuous longitudinal censorship measurement without in-country infrastructure.

milestones.title: Understanding Security Issues in the NFT Ecosystem
milestones.note: Characterized the full spectrum of NFT security issues including wash trading, scams, and smart contract vulnerabilities.

milestones.title: Empirical Analysis of EIP-1559: Transaction Fees, Waiting Times, and Consensus Security
milestones.note: Measured EIP-1559's real-world impact on Ethereum fee predictability and consensus security empirically.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this area treated cybercrime as an economy to be traced rather than just malware to be blocked. Two 2018 papers set the tone by following the money: "Tracking Ransomware End-to-end" (S&P 2018) tied infections to Bitcoin ransom flows to estimate how much victims actually paid, while "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) showed that even a privacy coin leaks deanonymizing patterns. Alongside this financial forensics, a parallel thread measured the abuse of everyday infrastructure — the mobile tracking ecosystem in "Apps, Trackers, Privacy, and Regulators" (NDSS 2018) and the rise of browser cryptojacking in "MineSweeper" (CCS 2018) and "How You Get Shot in the Back" (CCS 2018).

The field then broadened from "who profits" to "what ecosystems are exposed." In 2019, "Small World with High Risks" (USENIX 2019) recast abuse around software supply chains and npm's dependency graph, while "The Art of The Scam" (USENIX 2019) and "Cybercriminal Minds" (NDSS 2019) extended blockchain measurement to Ethereum honeypots and dark-web crypto abuse. Phishing became a measurement discipline of its own: "PhishFarm" (S&P 2019), "Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale" (USENIX 2019), and then the 2020 pair "Sunrise to Sunset" and "PhishTime" (both USENIX 2020) treated attacks as lifecycles to be timed against the defenses meant to stop them. Crucially, 2020 also pushed toward continuous, internet-wide instrumentation — "Censored Planet" (CCS 2020) turned censorship measurement into an always-on observatory, and studies like "Measuring and Modeling the Label Dynamics of Online Anti-Malware Engines" (USENIX 2020) interrogated the very data sources researchers rely on.

Two other shifts stand out. First, harm was reframed as social as well as financial: "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" (USENIX 2020) and "SoK: Hate, Harassment, and the Changing Landscape of Online Abuse" (S&P 2021) put interpersonal abuse squarely on the measurement agenda. Second, blockchains matured from a place to launder proceeds into an object of study in their own right — "Frontrunner Jones and the Raiders of the Dark Forest" (USENIX 2021), "Quantifying Blockchain Extractable Value" (S&P 2022), and "Understanding Security Issues in the NFT Ecosystem" (CCS 2022) measured extractive dynamics built into the protocols themselves rather than crimes layered on top.

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026, shows the area converging on planetary-scale ecosystem measurement and on the abuse-fighting infrastructure itself. "Hey there! You are using WhatsApp: Enumerating Three Billion Accounts" (NDSS 2026) demonstrates enumeration at the scale of an entire global platform, while "Beyond RTT" and "Aliens Among Us" (both NDSS 2026) probe residential-proxy and spoofed-IP abuse, and "On Borrowed Time" (NDSS 2026) stress-tests the NTP Pool's robustness. Notably, researchers are now turning the lens on the defensive ecosystem — "Tickets to Hide" (NDSS 2026) uses internal anti-abuse data, "Actively Understanding the Dynamics and Risks of the Threat Intelligence Ecosystem" (NDSS 2026) audits the threat-intel supply chain, and "NEXUS" (NDSS 2026) maps vulnerabilities to attack techniques — while "Revealing The Secret Power" and "TBTrackerX" (both NDSS 2026) measure algorithmic manipulation and bot campaigns on X. The through-line from 2018 to today is consistent: measure the whole ecosystem, at scale, longitudinally, and increasingly measure the mitigations as critically as the crimes.
